state.misconception_label: Assumes that an arrow on a number line starts at zero

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: ![Number line with -12 and -7 marked. Starting at -12, follow an arrow pointing to the right labelled +10. Then there is an arrow labelled b pointing to the left, which ends at -7 on the number line.]() What is the value of \( b \) ? I got \( -7 \) because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Why do you think the arrow starts at zero on the number line? Can you explain how you determined the value of \( b \) starting from -12?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Um, I think I just looked at where the arrow ended up, which was at -7, so I thought that was the answer. But now you're saying it doesn't start at zero... so does that mean I need to work out how far the arrow moves instead of just reading where it lands?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Can you think of a similar situation where you had to count backwards but didn't start at the initial number? How might that relate to determining the value of \( b \) on the number line from -12 to -7?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher directly addresses the zero-starting misconception and maintains high cognitive demand, but the final analogy in Turn 3 is vague and doesn't clearly connect to the problem, while the student shows partial progress by recognizing they need to calculate movement rather than just read endpoints.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses probing questions to guide the student's thinking without directly providing the answer, asking the student to explain their reasoning and make connections to similar situations, which is a textbook example of the Socratic method.
